First Customers in a Market That Doesn't Exist Yet

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 19 August 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Revenue

In a market that does not exist yet, first customers are chosen as design partners and references at once, bought through institutional procurement, reached through practitioner networks, and measured by risk retired. The institutions that buy first are slow for reasons that can be mapped in advance: procurement thresholds, security review, liability terms and planning calendars. Sandboxes and standards bodies are distribution as well as compliance, but they are selective: the UK Financial Conduct Authority accepted 14 of 142 sandbox applications in its 2025/26 financial year.

Design partners who are also references

Part 7 said the first ten customers are design partners. In long cycles that rule tightens. Each design partner costs a year or more of attention. You cannot afford one who shapes the product and then will not say so.

Choose design partners on three tests. They own the cost from Part 31. They can deploy in a setting that looks like the wider market. And they agree up front, in the pilot terms, to act as a reference if the agreed success criteria are met.

Write the success criteria into the pilot agreement. Vague pilots never end. Specific pilots convert or close, and both are useful. A mutual action plan is the working document: dated steps, an owner for each, and the reference commitment written in as a step rather than a hope.

Expect fewer partners than a software company would run. Three good ones, each in a different buyer type, teach more than ten shallow ones.

Pilots with governments, regulators, utilities and large corporates

These are the natural first buyers for robotics, infrastructure, energy, identity and verification. They are also the slowest. Four things differ from selling to a startup.

AreaWhat differsWhat to prepare
ProcurementFormal process, frameworks, thresholds, often tender rulesMap the route before first contact; find the threshold that allows a direct pilot
SecurityReview before any data or site accessSecurity pack, data handling, access controls, ready on day one
LiabilityRisk sits with the vendor; insurance and indemnity are negotiatedInsurance in place; a lawyer who has seen the buyer's standard terms
TimelinesBudget cycles, annual plans, committee calendarsKnow their planning calendar and work back from it

Thresholds are the first thing to check, because they decide whether a pilot can be bought quickly or must be tendered. In England, procurements starting on or after 1 January 2026 under the Procurement Act 2023 use a threshold of £135,018 including VAT for central government supplies and services, £207,720 for sub-central authorities, and £415,440 for utilities. Value is calculated including VAT, so a contract that looks under the line net of VAT can be over it. Other jurisdictions have their own figures. The point is the same everywhere: a pilot priced below the relevant threshold, with a clear scope, is a decision a budget holder can make; one above it is a process.

Security is the second. Institutions will expect the same questionnaires a large company sends, and often more. Our playbook on the pilot that survives security review sets out the pack, and our explainer on SOC 2 for AI vendors covers what a report does and does not prove.

The lesson is to sell the pilot as a project the institution can approve, not as a trial it can tolerate. That means a budget, a sponsor, a procurement route and an end date. Pilots without those are favours, and favours do not convert.

Part 4 said run the round like a sales process. Run institutional pilots the same way: stages, owners, exit criteria.

Pilots without a budget, a sponsor, a procurement route and an end date are favours, and favours do not convert.

Consortia and standards bodies as distribution

Part 8 said find channels that are open when platforms are closed. In emerging tech the open channel is often an industry consortium, a standards working group or a regulator's sandbox.

They are slow and unglamorous. They are also where the buyers sit when they are deciding what the category means. A company in the working group that writes the standard is a company every member has met.

AI is a live example. The European Commission asked CEN and CENELEC to develop harmonised standards for the AI Act in ten areas, from risk management and data governance to human oversight and quality management, and the work sits in their Joint Technical Committee 21. The first, EN 18286 on quality management systems for AI Act purposes, was published on 14 October 2026 and referenced in the Official Journal by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274. Applying harmonised standards is voluntary, but it gives a presumption of conformity, which is why buyers' compliance teams follow the committee's work closely. Our guide to the EU AI Act for commercial teams covers what applies and when.

Treat these bodies as distribution, not PR. Pick the one where your buyers are, not the one with the best logo. Send the person who can speak to the technical detail. Show up for the whole cycle, not the launch.

The same applies to regulator sandboxes. A sandbox place is a pilot with a clearance attached, which Part 32 said is a milestone. It is also competitive. The FCA's freedom of information response in May 2026 showed 142 applications and 14 acceptances in its 2025/26 financial year, and 52 applications with 16 acceptances the year before. Under the EU's amendments to the AI Act, member states' deadline to set up AI regulatory sandboxes moved to 2 August 2027, according to Gibson Dunn's summary of the agreement, so EU sandbox capacity is still being built.

ChannelWhat it gives youWhat it costsSelectivity
Industry consortiumAccess to members deciding what the category meansMembership fee and a senior person's timeUsually open to paying members
Standards working groupInfluence on requirements buyers will audit againstA technical expert for a multi-year cycleOpen through national standards bodies
Regulator sandboxA supervised pilot and a clearance signalApplication effort, reporting, constraints on scopeSelective: about one in ten at the FCA in 2025/26

The first hundred are practitioners, not a public community

Part 6 said the first hundred people are the ones who will tell others. Part 5 said community is a job. In emerging tech the hundred are not a public community at all.

They are the field engineers, grid operators, compliance leads, security researchers and procurement specialists who decide whether a new thing is credible. They do not gather on social platforms. They gather in working groups, technical forums, conferences with small audiences and private channels.

Build the list by name. Know what each person needs to see before they will vouch for you. Give it to them before you ask for anything.

Part 9 said stop reporting reach. Here that means a hundred practitioners who will return a call matters more than ten thousand followers who will not.

Measure progress by risk retired

Pipeline value is the wrong measure when deals take two years. A large pipeline of unconverted pilots is a cost, not an asset.

Measure what reduces risk. Technical milestones met in the field. Paid pilots signed and paid. Security reviews passed. Regulatory clearances won. References agreed in writing. Each one makes the next sale faster and the next raise cheaper.

Report those monthly, to the team and the board. Part 10's ten-question self-score works here with one change: replace revenue questions with risk-retired questions until revenue arrives.

CheckDone when
Design partnersEach owns the cost, resembles the wider market and has agreed in writing to be a reference
Pilot termsSuccess criteria, a sponsor, a budget and an end date
Institutional readinessProcurement route and threshold, security pack, insurance and timeline per buyer type
Open channelOne consortium, standards body or sandbox chosen where the buyers sit
PractitionersThe first hundred listed by name with what each needs to see
ReportingMonthly risk retired and paid pilots, not pipeline size

lowob takeaways

  • Choose design partners who will say so. They own the cost, resemble the market and agree in writing to be a reference.
  • Sell a project, not a trial. Budget, sponsor, procurement route and end date, priced with the threshold in mind.
  • Join where the category is defined. Standards bodies and sandboxes are distribution, and they are selective.
  • Report risk retired. Field milestones, paid pilots, security reviews, clearances and written references.

Common questions

How do I find first customers for a product in a brand-new market?

Choose a few design partners who own the cost, can deploy in a setting like the wider market, and agree up front to be references if agreed success criteria are met. Three good partners in different buyer types teach more than ten shallow ones.

How should a startup run a pilot with a government or large corporate?

Sell it as a project the institution can approve, with a budget, a sponsor, a procurement route and an end date. Check the procurement threshold first; in England the central government services threshold is £135,018 including VAT from January 2026.

Is it worth applying to a regulatory sandbox?

Often, if your buyers are regulated, because a sandbox place is a supervised pilot with a clearance signal. Expect competition: the FCA accepted 14 of 142 applications in 2025/26.

Are standards bodies worth a startup's time?

Yes, as distribution. They are slow, but buyers sit there while deciding what the category means. Pick the one where your buyers are and attend the whole cycle.

  • European Commission, Standardisation of the AI Act, as listed in November 2026. Official policy page; other harmonised standards are still in development.
  • Gibson Dunn, EU AI Act Omnibus Agreement: Postponed High-Risk Deadlines and Other Key Changes, 2026. Law firm analysis of the agreement later adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.
